# From findings to modeling decisions {#sec-eda-summary}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)

Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value
```

You now have a genuinely thick notebook on `cell_data`. Density plots, raincloud plots, a scatter you could hover over, a free-roaming session with GWalkR, a full correlation matrix. That's the same feeling I remember from the first pilot experiment I ever ran end to end: at the bench, the pilot's job isn't to answer the research question; it's to tell you what to change before you run the real thing. A page of pilot notes that never gets translated into "so here's what I'm doing differently" was wasted bench time, no matter how thorough it was. The same is true of an EDA notebook. This short chapter does that translation, once, for everything Part 2 has shown you, and in doing so, it finally keeps the promise made at the very start of this part: "the running list of things we now know about `cell_data` that will shape every modeling decision from here on."

## Three ways of looking, three kinds of evidence

I'm not going to repeat the five-bullet summary @sec-eda-ggplot already gave you about ranges, temporal trends, and covariance; go back to that chapter's closing section if you want the raw list again. What's worth naming here instead is that Part 2 didn't just repeat the same kind of look three times. Each chapter handed you a genuinely different *kind* of evidence, and knowing which kind you're holding matters for how much you trust it.

@sec-eda-ggplot gave you **directed evidence**: I picked the question, then picked the geometry that would answer it, and every conclusion is only as good as whether I picked the right question to ask. @sec-eda-gwalkr gave you **generated evidence**: hypotheses surfaced by dragging variables around with no question pre-loaded, which is exactly why it closed by handing you a specific hypothesis to go verify properly, rather than a conclusion. @sec-eda-ggpairs gave you **structural evidence**: not "what does one relationship look like," but "which variables in this whole dataset are secretly redundant," a question no amount of one-pair-at-a-time scatter plotting would have surfaced efficiently. Three different tools, three different jobs. None of them is a substitute for the others, which is exactly why the book walked through all three instead of stopping at the first one that felt sufficient.

## From findings to decisions

::: callout-note
### A naming note before the table

Two different arcs of this book have been using two different columns and calling them similar things, and I'd rather say that out loud than let you assume a contradiction. The worked example back in Part 1 used `Gfap_Intensity`, a per-animal intensity value. Part 2's EDA chapters have mostly worked with `Gfap_IntDen` and `Pdgfrb_IntDen`: integrated density, a related but distinct measurement. When a number below doesn't match a number from three chapters ago, that's why: different column, not a typo.
:::

Here's the table I actually sat down to build this chapter around: a map from what we saw to what we're going to do about it, and where in the book that gets handled. Read it as a table of contents for every modeling decision the rest of this book has already committed to making.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-eda_summary_decisions
#| tbl-cap: From EDA findings to modeling decisions

library(gt)

findings <- data.frame(
  finding = c(
    "Marker intensities are strictly positive and right-skewed, with spread that grows as the level grows",
    "Marker intensity rises non-linearly with DPI",
    "The spread of marker intensity is not constant across DPI (unequal variance)",
    "Pdgfrb_Area/Pdgfrb_IntDen and Gfap_Area/Gfap_IntDen are each highly correlated pairs",
    "The PDGFR-β/GFAP relationship changes shape across DPI",
    "SHAM animals exist only at DPI 0: a non-lesioned animal has no injury time course to measure",
    "Each row is one animal (49 rows, 49 unique MouseID); independence can't be read off a plot",
    "One value is missing (Pdgfrb_Neg, animal Td79), and the derived Pdgfrb_Total for that animal silently counted it as zero",
    "Tisue_Area duplicates Tissue_Area in µm² (factor 10^6), and Pdgfbr_MeanInt is a misspelled Pdgfrb_MeanInt"
  ),
  consequence = c(
    "A Gaussian likelihood is a convenient approximation here, not a given; worth revisiting once non-Gaussian families are on the table",
    "Violates the linearity assumption of a plain linear model",
    "Violates homoscedasticity; a constant-variance model would understate uncertainty at later DPI",
    "Including both members of a pair as predictors inflates standard errors (multicollinearity)",
    "A single additive slope undersells it; the model needs an interaction term, not just two main effects",
    "DPI is a meaningful injury-progression axis only within MCAO; SHAM is a deliberate baseline category, not a DPI level to blend in",
    "Independence is a design property, not a plot; it comes from knowing what a “row” actually is in this dataset",
    "A silent complete-case drop or an NA-propagating mean, plus one wrong-looking-fine derived total; whether it matters depends on why the value is missing, not on how many rows remain",
    "Keep Tissue_Area (mm²) and drop the µm² copy; the raw CSV and original names stay untouched, repairs live in a validated script (assertr rules)"
  ),
  where = c(
    "GLM chapters ahead in Part 3 (planned)",
    "Linearity: assumptions chapter (Part 3)",
    "Homoscedasticity: assumptions chapter (Part 3)",
    "Flagged here; quantified with VIF in the assumptions chapter (Part 3)",
    "Multiple regression chapter (planned, Part 3)",
    "Kept in mind for any SHAM+DPI model, e.g. the longitudinal chapter (planned, Part 4)",
    "Multilevel models chapter (planned, Part 4)",
    "Missing-data chapter, in this part",
    "Data-quality chapter, in this part"
  )
)
names(findings) <- c("What we saw", "Consequence for the model", "Where it's addressed")

gt(findings) |>
  cols_width(
    `What we saw` ~ pct(34),
    `Consequence for the model` ~ pct(38),
    `Where it's addressed` ~ pct(28)
  ) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(12)), locations = cells_body())
```

Three of those rows deserve more than one line, because the reasoning behind them is more interesting than the table lets on.

Take the redundant-predictor row first, since it's the newest finding. @sec-eda-ggpairs found it structurally: Pdgfrb_Area and Pdgfrb_IntDen, Gfap_Area and Gfap_IntDen, each pair carrying a Pearson correlation above 0.9. What EDA gave us there was the *fact* of the redundancy. What it deliberately didn't give us was a verdict, because there wasn't a model on the table yet to have a verdict about. @sec-linear-regression-assumptions is where that fact turns into a number you can act on: the variance inflation factor, computed on an actual fitted model, quantifying exactly how much that redundancy would distort a specific set of coefficients. Same finding, two different jobs: EDA screens for it, regression diagnostics quantify it once you've committed to a specific model.

Now the SHAM row, which I want to be precise about because it's easy to mischaracterize as a design flaw when it isn't one. SHAM animals appear only at DPI 0 in this dataset for a straightforward biological reason: a SHAM animal underwent the surgical procedure without the ischemic event itself, so there's no lesion, and therefore no injury time course to track: asking "what does a SHAM animal look like at 14 DPI" doesn't correspond to anything that happened. That's not a confound quietly waiting to bias a model; it's what the comparison *is*. It does mean, though, that DPI as a continuous predictor of injury progression only really applies within the MCAO animals, and that SHAM functions as a baseline category you invoke deliberately for a specific comparison, exactly how Part 1 used it, filtering to `DPI %in% c(0, 3)` to ask one clean question about the earliest post-ischemia window, rather than folding SHAM into a single DPI trend that spans the whole dataset. Worth keeping explicit the moment a future model tries to span both groups across the full time course at once.

Last, the independence row, because it's the one finding in this table that no amount of plotting could have surfaced. `cell_data` has 49 rows and 49 unique `MouseID` values: one row per animal, not repeated measurements of the same animal across time. At *this* level of aggregation, treating rows as independent observations is a reasonable starting assumption. But the roadmap for this book is explicit that a later chapter revisits the underlying per-cell measurements these per-animal numbers were built from (cells nested inside tissue sections nested inside animals), and that nesting is exactly the pseudoreplication problem Part 4's multilevel models chapter exists to solve. Nothing about the current summary table is wrong; it's just scoped to the data as it stands here, and I'd rather flag that boundary now than let you assume "independent" is a property of the biology rather than a property of how the spreadsheet in front of you happens to be organized.

## EDA as a habit, not a chapter

Here's something worth being honest about: everything in this part could have been sprinkled through Part 1 instead, a plot here and a distributional check there, right where each one was first needed. I didn't do it that way, and Part 1 told you so directly: @sec-mcmc-model-checking leaned on `brms`'s turnkey `pp_check()` specifically *because* the `ggplot2` fluency for building that comparison by hand hadn't been taught yet. That was a deliberate IOU, not an oversight, and this is where I pay it.

A posterior predictive check is, at its core, "does the shape of my model's simulated data resemble the shape of my real data", which is precisely the kind of visual comparison this part of the book has spent three chapters teaching you to build and to trust. Let's reload the informed model from @sec-priors-regularization (cached, no refitting) and rebuild that comparison ourselves instead of leaning on the turnkey version:

```{r}
#| label: fig-eda_summary_ppc_rebuild
#| fig-cap: A hand-built posterior predictive check for the informed ischemia model, echoing the pp_check() from mcmc-model-checking.qmd
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(here)
library(brms)

cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, DPI %in% c(0, 3))
cell_data_sub$Condition <- factor(cell_data_sub$Condition, levels = c("SHAM", "MCAO"))

priors_v1 <- c(
  prior(normal(30, 20), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 150), class = "b", coef = "ConditionMCAO"),
  prior(normal(0, 30), class = "sigma")
)

informed_fit <- brm(
  Gfap_Intensity ~ Condition,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  prior = priors_v1,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/priors-regularization_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

set.seed(8)
yrep <- posterior_predict(informed_fit, ndraws = 100)
yrep_df <- data.frame(
  value = as.vector(t(yrep)),
  draw = rep(seq_len(nrow(yrep)), each = ncol(yrep))
)

ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    data = yrep_df, aes(x = value, group = draw),
    color = "grey70", alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_density(
    data = cell_data_sub, aes(x = Gfap_Intensity),
    color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  labs(x = "GFAP intensity", y = "Density") +
  Plot_theme
```

That's a hundred faint grey curves, one per simulated dataset, with our real fifteen animals drawn as the single bold orange line, pushed to the background and highlighted deliberately (the same "grey the rest, accent the one thing that matters" move from @sec-eda-ggplot's own figures), applied here to a model's predictions instead of raw data. It's the identical comparison `pp_check(informed_fit, ndraws = 100)` made for you back in @sec-mcmc-model-checking, just assembled from the `ggplot2` primitives this part actually taught you, rather than a function you were asked to trust on faith. The point isn't that the hand-built version is somehow more correct (`pp_check()` was doing the same computation the whole time). It's that you can now see exactly what it was doing.

That's the real argument for treating EDA as a standing habit rather than a chapter you graduate from: @sec-priors-regularization's five-second glance at plausible GFAP values, done "to keep a prior honest," was already EDA, just not yet called by that name or given its own tools. A posterior predictive check is EDA turned on a model's output instead of on raw measurements. Once you've internalized "look before you trust," it doesn't stay confined to the chapter that first taught it to you.

## Opening the door to Part 3

Here's the shape of what changes from here. Everything in this part looked at `cell_data` *before* any model touched it: distributions, relationships, redundancies, all inspected on their own terms. Starting with @sec-linear-regression-what, we finally build a model and ask it to commit to a specific claim about those relationships. And the moment a model exists, the questions this part asked informally get formal names and formal tests: is the relationship actually linear (we already have reason to doubt it), is the variance actually constant (we already have reason to doubt that too), are the predictors actually independent of each other (two of ours, we now know precisely, are not). Every "we noticed X" in the table above is about to become "here's the assumption X violates, and here's what we do about it."

I'm not going to open that toolkit here: that's the next chapter's job, not this one's closing paragraph. What I want you carrying forward instead is simpler: nothing in the next part should surprise you. Every crack a regression diagnostic is about to find in `cell_data`, you already saw first, informally, with your own eyes, in this part of the book. That's exactly the order I wanted it in.
